name: Environmental monitoring and effluent reporting
summary: Every week an environmental technician samples each point where treated water leaves the site (the Mill polishing pond to Miron Creek and the mine settling ponds to Lake C7), records the flow and couriers the samples to an accredited laboratory in Thunder Bay; once a month a further sample goes to a toxicity laboratory in Oakville for fish and water-flea tests. The environmental coordinator checks the results against federal effluent limits and the provincial approvals, investigates high values with the mill, and files quarterly and annual reports. Most of the elapsed time is courier transit and laboratory turnaround; re-keying laboratory certificates into spreadsheets and the rare failed toxicity test, which triggers immediate notice and twice-monthly testing, are where errors and effort concentrate.

baseline.org_archetype: A single-mine Canadian gold producer running a 500-650 tpd underground mine and its own mill near Wawa in northern Ontario, with 12-hour shifts on 14-on/14-off rotations and a camp.
baseline.notes: Two final discharge points discharged through most of the year in 2019-2022 (Mill polishing pond and mine settling ponds), plus the Mishi pit ponds as needed in spring and fall until pit mining ended in 2020.

unit_of_work: one weekly effluent sampling event at one final discharge point, from bottle preparation to results recorded (and, for the last event of a quarter, the quarterly report filed)
trigger: The weekly sampling day for a final discharge point comes up on the monitoring schedule.
end_state: The laboratory results are reviewed and stored for regulatory reporting, any exceedance or lethal result has been notified and followed up, and at quarter end the report is filed.

volume.seasonality: Weekly sampling continues all year. The Mill discharge is lower or stopped in February-March and August-September, and the Mishi pit ponds discharged mainly in spring and fall while the pit operated (to 2020), adding a third point in those months.

evidence.note: Two continuously discharging final discharge points sampled weekly (MDMER s. 12) give about 8.7 events a month; the Mishi pit ponds add up to 4 a month when discharging. The organisation file's 4-10 (mode 6) is low for two points sampled weekly.

surge.cause: Spring freshet and fall discharge from the Mishi pit settling ponds, adding a third final discharge point

evidence.note: The technical report says the Mishi pit ponds discharged as needed, primarily in spring and fall, during pit operations; durations are the author's estimate. Applies to 2019-2020 only.

Two technicians on a 14/14 rotation give one on site; weekly effluent sampling, packing and data entry take about half of that person's time, with groundwater, receiving-water and tailings inspection work on top.
Two coordinators; about a third of one person's time goes to effluent review and reporting, the rest to permits, closure plans and EEM studies.
Approves quarterly and annual reports and handles escalations.
Treatment changes after high results.

systems.name: Environmental monitoring data workbooks and lab certificates
Shared drives and document library (procedures, permits, drawings)
Leaky feeder radio and surface radio network
Mill distributed control system and process historian

resources.name: Environmental department pickup truck (snowmobile in winter)

steps.name: Plan the sampling round and prepare bottles
steps.description: The environmental technician checks the monitoring schedule in the environmental data workbook to see which final discharge point is due, whether this is the monthly toxicity week, and which receiving-water stations ride along. They take pre-labelled, pre-preserved bottles from the laboratory's kit, fill out field sheets and chain-of-custody forms, and calibrate the field pH and temperature meter.

error.defect_description: Wrong bottle set or preservative for a parameter, or the meter is not calibrated.

evidence.note: Weekly sampling of each final discharge point at least 24 hours apart is set by MDMER s. 12(1); preparation time and the wait for the scheduled sampling day are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Drive to the final discharge point
steps.description: The technician drives the site pickup to the discharge point, either the Mill polishing pond outlet to Miron Creek or the mine water settling ponds at Lake C7, a few kilometres apart on site roads. In winter the last stretch may need a snowmobile, and a storm or road plowing can hold the trip for a day.

evidence.note: Discharge points and receiving waters from section 20.4 of the Eagle River technical report; drive time and weather delay are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Read the flow meter and record discharge volume
steps.description: The technician reads the totalizer and instantaneous flow on the effluent flow meter or weir, writes them on the field sheet with the time, and notes anything unusual such as a frozen weir or a pump not running. The readings feed the monthly volume that the quarterly report needs.

error.defect_description: Totalizer misread or meter not working, leaving a gap in the monthly volume.

control.basis: MDMER s. 19: record the monthly volume of effluent from each final discharge point with a flow monitoring system accurate to 15% and calibrated yearly

evidence.note: Volume recording rule from MDMER s. 19; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect grab samples and take field readings
steps.description: The technician fills the bottles for metals, total cyanide, total suspended solids and ammonia at the outlet, adds or checks preservatives, measures pH and temperature in the field, and takes a duplicate or field blank on the scheduled weeks. Each bottle gets the date, time and station on its label.

error.defect_description: Sample taken from the wrong point, preservative missed or label error.

control.basis: MDMER s. 12(1): grab or composite sample of each final discharge point at least once a week for pH and the prescribed deleterious substances

next.condition: monthly acute lethality week (one sampling event in about 4.3)

evidence.note: Parameters and frequency from MDMER ss. 12-14; the 0.23 share is one lethality sample a month over 4.3 weekly events; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect the acute lethality sample and pack both sample sets
steps.description: In the monthly toxicity week the technician also fills clean containers with effluent for the rainbow trout and Daphnia magna tests, then packs the toxicity containers and the chemistry bottles in separate coolers with ice packs and fills in a chain-of-custody form for each laboratory.

error.defect_description: Toxicity sample volume short or container not cooled, so the laboratory cannot run the test.

control.basis: MDMER s. 14(1): monthly grab sample from each final discharge point for acute lethality tests on rainbow trout (s. 14.1) and Daphnia magna (s. 14.3)

evidence.note: Monthly lethality sampling and test species from MDMER ss. 14-14.3; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Preserve and pack the chemistry samples
steps.description: Back at the environmental office the technician checks every bottle against the chain-of-custody form, keeps cyanide and ammonia bottles cold, packs them in a cooler with ice packs and books the courier pickup at the gatehouse.

error.defect_description: Bottle missing from the form or cooler not cold enough on arrival.

evidence.note: Standard chain-of-custody practice for regulated effluent samples sent to a commercial laboratory; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Courier carries the chemistry cooler to the laboratory
steps.description: The courier picks up the cooler at the site gate and takes it by road from near Wawa to the accredited water laboratory in Thunder Bay. Samples taken late in the week miss the pickup and wait at site, kept cold, until the next run.

evidence.note: Water and effluent analyses by Testmark Laboratories in Thunder Bay (technical report section 11.2); courier time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Courier carries both coolers to the two laboratories
steps.description: In the toxicity week the courier takes the chemistry cooler to Thunder Bay and the toxicity cooler to the toxicity laboratory in Oakville in southern Ontario. Toxicity samples must arrive cold and within the holding time, so the technician times sampling to the courier run.

evidence.note: Toxicity tests by Nautilus Environmental in Oakville (technical report section 11.2); transit time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Laboratory analyses the weekly chemistry samples
steps.description: The laboratory logs the samples, checks temperature and holding times, runs metals by ICP, cyanide, suspended solids and ammonia, and emails a certificate of analysis as a PDF and spreadsheet. A sample that arrives warm or past its holding time is rejected and the mine must resample.

evidence.note: Routine turnaround of five to ten days at commercial environmental laboratories; the rejection share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Laboratory analyses the chemistry samples from the toxicity week
steps.description: The water laboratory runs the same weekly chemistry on the samples from the toxicity week and emails the certificate. The work runs at the same time as the toxicity tests in Oakville.

evidence.note: Same turnaround estimate as step s09.

steps.name: Toxicity laboratory runs rainbow trout and Daphnia tests
steps.description: The toxicity laboratory sets up the 96-hour rainbow trout test and the 48-hour Daphnia magna test on the undiluted effluent, records mortality, and issues a report stating whether the sample was acutely lethal. A lethal result is phoned or emailed to the environmental coordinator the day it is read.

control.basis: MDMER ss. 14.1 and 14.3: acute lethality tests on rainbow trout and Daphnia magna by the reference methods

next.condition: acutely lethal: more than 50% of test organisms died

evidence.note: The 96-hour and 48-hour test lengths follow the reference methods MDMER cites; report turnaround and the share of failed tests are the author's estimates (the technical report says 2020 effluent met all MDMER limits).

steps.name: Enter laboratory results and compare them with the limits
steps.description: The technician copies the certificate values into the environmental data workbook, flags any value above the MDMER Schedule 4 limits or the ECA effluent limits and objectives, and files the PDF certificate with the field sheet.

error.defect_description: Value re-keyed wrongly or unit mixed up (mg/L against ug/L).

evidence.note: Re-keying of laboratory certificates into spreadsheets was common practice in 2019-2022; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review results and quality-control samples
steps.description: The environmental coordinator reviews the week's results against the limits and against previous weeks, checks duplicates and blanks, and decides whether a high value is real or a sampling or laboratory error that needs a resample.

next.condition: a value above an ECA objective or limit

evidence.note: The technical report records 2020 Mill results above ECA objectives for copper, free cyanide and un-ionized ammonia; branch shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Add the results to the quarterly reporting file
steps.description: The coordinator moves the reviewed results and flow into the quarterly MDMER tables and the ECA annual summary in the workbook so that the reports can be assembled at quarter end.

control.basis: MDMER s. 27: monitoring records kept at the mine for at least five years

next.condition: last sampling event of the quarter: quarterly report due

evidence.note: Record retention from MDMER s. 27; the 0.08 share is one event in about 13 per quarter.

steps.name: Investigate the high value with the mill
steps.description: The coordinator phones the mill superintendent or metallurgist, looks at pond levels, hydrogen peroxide dosing in the reclaim pond and recent process upsets, and decides whether the result breaches a compliance limit that must be reported or only an objective.

next.condition: objective only or explained by sampling

evidence.note: Cyanide treatment with hydrogen peroxide in the reclaim pond is described in technical report section 17; investigation time and branch shares are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Notify the ministry district office of the exceedance
steps.description: The coordinator phones and emails the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks district office as the ECA requires, giving the parameter, value, likely cause and the action under way, after the HSE manager has seen the draft.

control.basis: Environmental Compliance Approval conditions for the Mill and mine sewage works: notice to the ministry district office of an effluent limit exceedance

evidence.note: ECAs for mine sewage works commonly require prompt notice of limit exceedances; the ECA text itself was not opened.

steps.name: Adjust treatment or hold back discharge
steps.description: The mill superintendent has the shift raise peroxide dosing, slow the discharge pump or recirculate water to the tailings area until levels fall, and tells the coordinator when the change is in place.

evidence.note: The technical report describes controlled-rate discharge from the polishing pond and peroxide treatment; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect a confirmation sample
steps.description: The technician returns to the discharge point, takes a confirmation sample for the parameter that was high plus the routine set, and sends it for rush analysis.

evidence.note: Confirmation sampling after an exceedance is common practice; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Notify an inspector of the acutely lethal effluent
steps.description: As soon as the laboratory reports a lethal result the coordinator phones and emails the federal enforcement officer or inspector, and tells the mill to review the discharge. The call is made the same day.

control.basis: MDMER s. 24(1): notify an inspector without delay when an effluent is acutely lethal

evidence.note: Notification rule from MDMER s. 24(1); minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Brief the general manager and corporate office
steps.description: The HSE manager briefs the general manager and the chief operating officer on the failed test, the likely cause and whether discharge should be stopped, and agrees who will speak to the ministry and local First Nations if asked.

evidence.note: Escalation path is the author's description of common practice at a listed single-mine producer.

steps.name: Characterize the effluent and test twice a month
steps.description: The technician takes effluent characterization samples at once, then lethality samples twice a month at least seven days apart until three in a row pass. Each round repeats the sampling, packing and courier steps; the elapsed time is mostly waiting for test results.

control.basis: MDMER s. 15: effluent characterization and lethality tests twice a month until three consecutive non-lethal results

evidence.note: Increased testing rule from MDMER s. 15; hands-on minutes cover three to four extra sampling rounds and are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the 30-day report on the lethal result
steps.description: The coordinator writes the follow-up report with the test results, characterization data, the cause found and the corrective action, has the HSE manager sign it and sends it to the inspector.

control.basis: MDMER s. 24(2): written report within 30 days after the lethality testing is completed

evidence.note: Report deadline from MDMER s. 24(2); drafting time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Compile the quarterly effluent monitoring report
steps.description: After the quarter ends the coordinator totals monthly volumes, calculates monthly mean concentrations and loadings for each final discharge point, lists the lethality test results and enters everything into the federal online reporting system, with a matching summary for the provincial ECA file.

error.defect_description: Monthly mean or loading miscalculated from the workbook.

control.basis: MDMER s. 21(1): effluent monitoring report for each calendar quarter within 45 days after the quarter ends

evidence.note: Quarterly deadline from MDMER s. 21(1); the wait runs from the last weekly event to the reporting work near the deadline, and drafting time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review and approve the report
steps.description: The HSE manager reads the draft, checks any exceedance against the notices already sent and the corrective actions, and approves it for submission or returns it with corrections.

control.basis: Company sign-off of regulatory submissions by the HSE manager

next.condition: fourth quarter: annual reports also due

evidence.note: Sign-off by the site HSE manager is common practice; shares follow one annual report per four quarterly reports.

steps.name: Submit the report to the federal and provincial regulators
steps.description: The coordinator submits the quarterly report in the federal online system, emails the ECA summary to the ministry district office where required, and saves the confirmation in the permit file.

evidence.note: Submission duties from MDMER ss. 21 and 22; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Compile the annual MDMER and ECA reports
steps.description: For the fourth quarter the coordinator also writes the annual MDMER report and the annual ECA monitoring reports for the Mill and the mine, with the year's results, flow totals, exceedances, groundwater results and corrective actions, due by March 31.

control.basis: MDMER s. 22: annual report by March 31 for the previous calendar year; ECA annual reporting conditions

evidence.note: Annual deadline from MDMER s. 22; the technical report cites the Mill, Mishi pit and mine 2020 annual reports; drafting time is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Acutely lethal toxicity result
exceptions.description: About 4% of monthly toxicity samples (one event in 4.3) fail; the inspector is notified the same day, the effluent is characterized and tested twice a month until three tests pass, and a written report follows within 30 days.

exceptions.name: Effluent value above an ECA objective or limit
exceptions.description: A copper, cyanide or ammonia value is above an objective or limit; the coordinator investigates with the mill, notifies the ministry if a limit is breached, and confirms with a resample.

exceptions.name: Sample rejected or quality-control failure
exceptions.description: The laboratory rejects a warm or late sample, or a duplicate or blank fails, and the round is repeated.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from sampling day to results reviewed and stored (quarter-end events include the report)
benchmarks.population: Weekly effluent sampling at an Ontario gold mine using a commercial laboratory about 500 km away by road

evidence.note: One to two days of courier transit and five to ten days of laboratory turnaround, plus a few days of review; quarter-end events wait up to the 45-day MDMER deadline.

benchmarks.unit: days after the end of the quarter

evidence.note: MDMER s. 21(1).

benchmarks.unit: tests per year per final discharge point (before any reduction)

evidence.note: Monthly testing under MDMER s. 14(1); quarterly allowed after 12 passing months under s. 16.

pain_points.description: Laboratory certificates are re-keyed into spreadsheets and then re-keyed again into the federal reporting system, so transcription errors surface only at quarter-end review.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice in 2019-2022.

pain_points.description: Samples travel about 500 km to Thunder Bay and further to Oakville; a missed courier run or a warm cooler costs a week and a repeat trip.

evidence.note: Laboratory locations from the technical report; the delay effect is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: With one technician on site per rotation, sampling competes with groundwater, receiving-water and tailings inspections, and winter access to the discharge points can slip a day.

evidence.note: Organisation file headcount (two technicians on 14/14) and author's estimate.

sources.title: Metal and Diamond Mining Effluent Regulations (SOR/2002-222), full text
sources.publisher: Government of Canada, Justice Laws Website
sources.supports: s. 12(1): sample each final discharge point at least once a week, at least 24 hours apart, for pH and the prescribed deleterious substances; s. 13: reduction to quarterly for some substances after 12 months below 10% of the limit; s. 14(1): monthly acute lethality grab sample, at least 15 days apart, tested on rainbow trout (s. 14.1) and Daphnia magna (s. 14.3); s. 15(1): after a lethal result, effluent characterization without delay and lethality tests twice a month at least seven days apart, back to monthly after three consecutive non-lethal tests (s. 15(2)); s. 19: monthly effluent volume, flow monitoring accurate to 15% and calibrated yearly; s. 21(1): quarterly report within 45 days after the quarter; s. 22: annual report by March 31; s. 24: notify an inspector without delay of an acutely lethal effluent and give a written report within 30 days after testing; s. 27: records kept at the mine for five years.

sources.title: Technical Report for the Eagle River Gold Mining Complex, Ontario, Canada (NI 43-101)
sources.publisher: SRK Consulting (Canada) Inc. for Wesdome Gold Mines Ltd.
sources.supports: Section 20.4: monitoring under the ECAs, the PTTW and the MDMER covers effluent flow and quality during discharge, effluent toxicity tests, groundwater and receiving water; treated effluent from the Mill polishing pond to Miron Creek is discharged at controlled rates through most of the year, with little or none in February-March and August-September; the Eagle River Mine settling ponds discharge continuously to Lake C7; the Mishi pit ponds discharged to Macassa Creek as needed, mainly in spring and fall, during pit operations; 2020 annual reports met MDMER and ECA limits, with copper, free cyanide and un-ionized ammonia above ECA objectives at the Mill and one monthly dissolved aluminum exceedance at Mishi; EEM biological studies every three years. Section 11.2: water and effluent analyses by Testmark Laboratories (Thunder Bay, ISO 17025 accredited through CALA) and toxicity tests by Nautilus Environmental (Oakville). Section 17: cyanide in reclaim pond water treated with hydrogen peroxide. Table 20-1: Mill ECA peak flow 4,750 m3/day. Section 18 lists a warehouse among site buildings.

assumptions: The unit of work is one weekly sampling event at one final discharge point; monthly toxicity tests ride on one event in about 4.3, and the quarterly report is attached to the last event of each quarter (share 0.08), so the cycle-time median describes ordinary weekly events.

The organisation file describes 'batch releases'; the Eagle River technical report says Mill effluent is discharged at controlled rates through most of the year and the mine settling ponds discharge continuously, so batch-release approval is not modelled as a step.

The second final discharge point (mine settling ponds to Lake C7) is fed by mine dewatering, so triggered_by names mine-dewatering beside mill-water-treatment. Laboratory results are treated as an input returned within the case rather than a trigger.
Toxicity sampling is modelled on its own path (s05, s08, s10, s11) so that only toxicity-week events wait for toxicity results; s11 runs alongside s10.
The simulated median of about 14 days is close to the 12-day estimate; the extra days come from the long tail of laboratory turnaround (s09, s10) and review queues.
Receiving-water, groundwater and EEM biological sampling (every three years) are outside this unit of work and not modelled.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's rates: base wage times 1.30 for office and staff roles and 1.35 for hourly site roles.
The ECA notification step (s16) rests on common ECA conditions; the ECA texts were not opened.
